paragraphs: In the spring of Jianyuan’s twelfth year, the water on Xiliu Plain rose past the horses’ hooves.

A single night of rain had turned the camp of thirty thousand into a brown marsh. Before dawn a packhorse sank into the mire west of the camp. The harder it struggled, the deeper it went, until mud filled its nostrils. Several Qiang soldiers looped a rope around its neck and hauled until the cords stood out on their forearms. Two Han carpenters came running, abandoned their axes, and wedged a cartwheel beneath the animal’s belly. By the time they dragged it free, the rope had nearly strangled it.
Liang Hu stood nearby, plastered with mud to the waist. “Those lucky bastards with tents on high ground. Why do we have to be the first to rot our feet?”

Manu was loosening the knot at the horse’s neck. He raised two fingers toward Liang Hu. Zhao An translated: “He says he told you to dig a ditch beside your tent. You refused. Said he was trying to mark a river through Di territory.”
Liang Hu rolled his eyes. “My ditch would have drained water for you too.”
“Then dig it,” Zhao An said.

When Murong Chui arrived, the five men were arguing with a broken spade handle over who should cut the first channel. He had his robe gathered up, mud thick on his boots, and several squad leaders trailing behind him, none prepared to yield to the others. The Xianbei cavalry wanted their stables moved uphill. The Han soldiers demanded the main drain be opened first. The Di troops insisted that the granary came before everything. Murong Chui listened, then planted his measuring staff into the standing water.
“More rain from the northwest tonight. Whichever tents drain first will draw dry fodder first tomorrow morning.”

He turned and left. The squad leaders argued a while longer, then picked up their spades. By afternoon, channels that had begun in separate corners of the camp had joined. Muddy water rushed into an abandoned streambed, exposing patches of black earth. Manu tossed a hard flatbread across the ditch to Liang Hu. Liang Hu caught it and ate two bites before noticing the muddy fingerprints still on its crust.
It was then that the carriage escort of Fu Rong, Prince of Yangping, reached the camp gate.

He carried a frontier dispatch from Hexi. The cover had been soaked by the courier’s sweat and the rain; its wax seal remained intact. Murong Chui had read barely half when Liang Hu, lowering his bread, saw the ease leave the general’s face.

West of Wushi, Liangzhou border cavalry had fallen upon a caravan in which merchants traveled alongside refugees. Of eighty Qin escorts, fifty-seven were killed; more than three hundred merchants and civilians lay dead, and over seven hundred had been carried away. An attached burial list gave the names and native places of those identified. Its last line read: “Sixteen women and men, unnamed.” A fingernail had torn the paper beside the words.
“On orders from the Liang court?” Murong Chui asked.

“The border commanders are taking grain wherever they please. Jincheng calls it private raiding; Wuwei claims the Qin merchants crossed the frontier first.” Fu Rong’s jaw tightened. “Their statements contradict each other. The villages they burned cannot leave their dead unburied while we wait for the stories to agree.”
“You have come to send me west?”
“I have come to ask you back to court.”
Murong Chui folded the report. Outside, the men digging drains were still shouting. They knew nothing of the dead in Hexi, or that their own names might soon appear on another military dispatch.
“Half a year of drilling, and they have only just learned to stop when someone orders them to stop,” Murong Chui said. “Now we must put them in a real battle.”
Fu Rong glanced toward the door. “You fear they cannot win?”
“I fear that once they do win, they will remember which army each of them came from.”

Three days later, war was debated in Chang’an. The voices at court rang in much neater order than the spades on Xiliu Plain. Fu Pi asked for a hundred thousand troops to settle Liang in a single campaign. Veteran princes volunteered for the vanguard; some were already arguing over who would govern Guzang when it fell. A junior officer of the Secretariat hesitated and observed that relay stations along the route were in disrepair, the spring shortage was not yet over, and the stores for a hundred thousand soldiers existed only on paper. Before he could finish, someone accused him of fearing battle.
Fu Jian did not lose his temper. He had a map of Hexi spread across the great table and ordered the provision officers to read their figures aloud.
“One army of thirty thousand. Two months' rations. Fourteen thousand horses and six thousand pack animals. How many fighting men, wagonwrights, pass guards, and sick or wounded does that leave?”

The officer’s voice sank when he came to the civilian porters. The original proposal called for twenty thousand. Fu Rong, using what the counties could actually spare, reduced the figure to eight thousand. With so few shoulders, grain could not be carried all the way west; moving it by other means required depots along the road. An army could not fly straight to Guzang like a thrown knife.
“Speed is the soul of war,” Fu Pi said. “Liang is divided. Three months would suffice—”
“From which day do your three months begin?” Murong Chui interrupted.
“From the day we march, of course.”

“And if Guzang’s northern gate holds, and the city has food for four months, where will you find your three? If the Liang commanders withdraw to the western prefectures, will you pursue them, or leave thirty thousand men feeding horses outside an empty city?”
Fu Pi flushed. “The Champion General was fond of unexpected maneuvers when he served Yan. Now he has learned to calculate on behalf of Liang.”
Murong Chui regarded him. “In Yan, men often said the next battle would take no more than three months. In the end it was Yan that did not live to see them pass.”

Silence fell around the table. From the head of the hall Fu Jian looked at the former Prince of Wu. Fu Pi still gripped his court tablet so tightly that the veins rose on the back of his hand. His father did not rescue him. After a moment he stepped back into rank.
“Hong, what of the grain routes you examined last night?” Fu Jian asked.

Fu Hong produced two roughly bound ledgers. One came from the Guanzhong transport office; the other was a record kept by porters along the relay road. The totals did not agree. Rather than make them match, he had noted where beasts had been lost, where rain had blocked the road, and where relay workers had fled.

“For a hundred thousand men, even the human rations alone are heavy, before horse fodder is counted. Under the old reckoning, ten measures dispatched to Hexi arrived as five at best. Several depot roads are damaged this year. We may not keep even that much.” He paused. “I cannot find the grain for a campaign to destroy Liang in three months. Yet if more frontier families are taken captive, there may be no one left to till the fields west of Wushi this autumn.”
Fu Jian pushed the ledgers toward the ministers and ordered them passed down the hall.

“I do not blame you for wanting Liangzhou. But whoever asks for a hundred thousand men shall sign his name in these books. The counties that go short of grain, the men summoned to carry it: come autumn, they should know whom to thank.”

No one came forward to sign. Outside the hall a line of palace servants carried freshly washed draperies past the doors. Water dripped steadily from the cloth onto the stone path. Every minister could hear it.

In the end, Fu Jian ordered the First Battalion to march west. Thirty thousand under Murong Chui would secure three dangerous frontier passes, recover the abducted people, and intercept Liang cavalry crossing the border. They were not to attack Guzang without authorization, nor to pursue a city for its own sake into Liang’s interior. If Liangzhou garrisons sought terms, the Qin troops would first receive the captives, verify the enemy’s documents, and send the matter back to the Secretariat. Army stores were to be checked by both Central Military Command and the Secretariat. Commanders might act as necessity required in battle, but they must give a full account afterward. The last clause was added in the emperor’s own hand: when townspeople sought protection in great numbers, troops could shelter them temporarily; they could not change a prefecture’s allegiance without a new imperial decree.

Many generals were disappointed when the edict had been read. Thirty thousand troops sent west without permission to take all of Hexi seemed, to them, a sword polished bright and forbidden to cut. Murong Chui studied the wording more closely. He read the provision about temporarily protecting lives twice, folded the decree, and put it inside his armor pouch.
Yao Chang had remained to one side of the hall. When the ministers were about to disperse, he asked leave to join the expedition.
“The Right Guard’s duties at the palace have only just been settled,” Fu Jian said. “It cannot spare its commander.”
“I know the tribes of Hexi, Your Majesty. I know their roads.”
“I know you do. That is why you will stay.”

The words were quietly spoken. Yet to Yao Chang they were more humiliating than the day he had lost his troops. The emperor would not restore his old Qiang army, but would entrust thirty thousand new soldiers to Murong Chui. That man had once lost a kingdom, had known the desire to rebel, and still had countless Yan people waiting for his return.
Yao Chang bowed. “I obey. But many Qiang serve in this army, and the families of old comrades remain in the capital. If they lack grain or cloth, may I continue looking after them?”
“You may. Submit their names to the Secretariat. Every payment goes through the public accounts.”
“I understand.”

After court, Yao Chang returned to the Right Guard office and sorted the petitions for family relief. He recognized the surnames in the handwriting, remembered whose fathers and brothers had once shielded him from blades. His deputy asked whether the grain deliveries should bear the general’s private seal, so that the recipients would know who had done them a kindness. Yao Chang lifted his brush, then set it down.
“If the grain never reaches them, what good is knowing my name? Use the court forms.”

He gave that order, yet told the deputy to make a separate copy of the families' addresses and hide it at the bottom of a chest. It was one last thin thread from a lifetime of old allegiance. He had not decided when to cut it.

In the twelve days before departure, the First Battalion repaired wagons, selected horses, stitched saddles, and counted pay. Murong Chui kept veterans whose old wounds had reopened in the capital district and filled their places with trained reserves. Some thought he was casting the old soldiers aside. They came to the camp gate and begged on their knees. One white-bearded Xianbei horseman said he had followed the Prince of Wu since the days of Yan; if he could not go now, he might never again ride to a battlefield in Hexi.
Murong Chui did not help him to his feet. He ordered a spare horse brought out.
“Mount. Ride three circuits of the camp.”

The old man dragged himself into the saddle. Halfway around the second circuit, his injured right leg cramped. His body tipped sideways; he nearly fell. Murong Chui caught the reins and helped him down. The man’s face turned ashen. He thought the general would never look at him again.
“Stay behind and train the horses for me,” Murong Chui said. “The new mounts understand only Xianbei. Who knows them better than you?”
The old soldier stared, then slowly straightened.
“My lord... I accept.”

The country to which this army was going lay far beyond the plain where it had been formed. The departure rolls still counted thirty thousand, but that number included storehouse guards, cart crews, scouts, and supply units. All thirty thousand could never stand in one battle line. Murong Chui entered the distinction in three separate registers. He did not want the court to see only the figure and imagine that every soldier could cross a mountain pass at once.

Fu Hong sat outside his tent verifying the beneficiaries of the last men’s death allowances. Zhao An had listed his family carefully, parents, wife, and children. Manu’s mother moved with the grazing herds; six months ago she had been in Longyou, but now his entry for home district remained blank. Liang Hu had an army allotment of land but no kin to whom he could entrust it. The clerk pressed him to supply a name. After a long while he pointed to the five men behind him.
“If I die, give the money to whichever of them brings my sword home.”
“Public money cannot be given away on a whim,” the clerk said sternly.
Fu Hong was checking another roll. He looked up. “Have you truly no family, Liang Hu, or do you not wish to look for them?”

Liang Hu lowered his head and rubbed the mud on his knee with his knuckles. Once, he had carried the clothes of a fallen comrade back to an old woman who wept too hard to make a sound. His own home had burned in war ten years before.
“I did,” he said.

Fu Hong asked nothing more. He told the clerk to attach a separate agreement concerning personal effects, witnessed by the man’s squadmates. If no family claimed them, they would be held by the military burial office after the campaign. The clerk muttered about the trouble and filled in the form. When Zhai Hei’s turn came, he could not even be certain of the year of his birth. Suddenly he drew a half-ring of bronze from his clothing. His elder sister had given it to him. If anyone ever recognized it, he said, the rest of his possessions should go to her. No one felt like laughing now.

There was no wine in the camp on the eve of departure. The supply officers issued an extra piece of dried meat and filled the water skins of every cooking group. Qifu Wu grabbed the largest piece and ran, Manu chasing him halfway around the camp. With his back to the fire, Zhao An sharpened his sword for a long time, then asked Liang Hu, “If Guzang really opens its gates, do we go home to Chang’an?”
“The decree says we aren’t attacking Guzang.”
“It doesn’t say Guzang can’t open its gates by itself.”

Liang Hu made no answer. He watched the Qin banner hanging above the camp. If Helai Yan were alive, he would probably have laughed at Zhao An’s worrying and dragged them off to inspect the new saddles. But he lay buried outside Chang’an now, and the short wolf-tooth knife he had left behind was evidence in a case still unsolved. Liang Hu touched the grip of his own sword, worn smooth in one shallow groove by sweat. The memory of his dead Xianbei squadmate stopped his hand.

At the hour of Mao the next morning, Ba Bridge was cleared for the army. Supply carts stretched for miles along the bending river; pack bells and hoofbeats merged into a single rolling sound. The people of Chang’an crowded the roadside. When they saw Xianbei cavalry they shouted, “The Yan army!” When Qiang archers passed, they called out, “The Qiang!” When Liang Hu’s squad came by, an old flatbread seller craned his neck and declared, “Here come the Di!” No one shouted Qifu Wu’s own people’s name, so he made a face at the crowd, sending the children into peals of laughter.

Murong Chui dismounted west of the bridge to take leave of his emperor. Fu Jian wore an old purple cloak; the wind snapped its hem about his legs. For a moment they stood several paces apart as they had on the day Murong Chui first entered Chang’an. Only now there were no scattered soldiers of the fallen Yan and no frightened families behind him, but ranks of Qin troops, still not quite straight.
“If Guzang opens its gates?” Fu Jian asked.
“Protect the people first. Wait for the court’s decision.”
“And if the grain runs out?”
“Withdraw.”
“If you cannot bear to give up the city before your eyes?”
Murong Chui gave the faintest smile. “Your Majesty once found it hard to part with my tiger tally. Surely I may be allowed to find something hard to part with today.”

Fu Jian did not smile. He handed Murong Chui a sealed wooden casket. Inside lay proclamations for the Liangzhou frontier officials and credentials for envoys to the prefectures, together with blank forms for reporting their findings. Generals rarely cared for such things. Far from home, they might keep many people from dying without anyone ever knowing why.
“Win battles for me,” he said. “And write down the names of those you fail to bring back.”
Murong Chui received the casket in both hands and bowed toward the eastern side of the bridge.

At last the drums sounded. The First Battalion’s vanguard crossed the Ba River, while the rear columns slowly wound west through the bends of the valley. Sunlight broke through the cloud and struck the red edge of the Qin banner until it gleamed like a thread of molten gold. Fu Jian watched until the flags had dwindled to pinpricks in the yellow dust.
Fu Hong stood behind his father. “If these thirty thousand win, will the realm believe in the new army?”
“Winning is the easier part,” Fu Jian replied. “The hard thing is whether, when they come back, they will still be willing to walk beside the men who crossed this bridge with them today.”

The gates of Chang’an had closed in the distance. Spring water rushed east beneath the bridge, while the horses bound west did not turn back. Only after the crowd had dispersed did Yao Chang depart. He walked alone past the Right Guard barracks and heard someone in the office singing an old song softly in the Qiang tongue. He stopped for one step. He gave no order to silence it.
The west wind soon carried the singing away.
